questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of the two pointers technique on sorted arrays?

options.text: It eliminates nested loops and finds pairs in O(n) linear time.
options.explanation: Right. Two pointers move across the array in one pass, reducing quadratic time to linear.

options.text: It converts arrays into binary trees for logarithmic lookups.
options.explanation: Two pointers work directly on arrays without constructing tree structures.

options.text: It guarantees thread-safe mutations during concurrent operations.
options.explanation: Two pointers is an algorithmic pattern, not a concurrency primitive.

options.text: It eliminates the need for array boundary checks completely.
options.explanation: The algorithm still requires checking boundary conditions like left < right.

questions.prompt: In a convergent two-pointer Two Sum on a sorted array, what do you do if current sum < target?

options.text: Decrement the right pointer to inspect a smaller element.
options.explanation: Decrementing right reduces the sum further, moving away from target.

options.text: Increment the left pointer to increase the total sum.
options.explanation: Right. Because the array is sorted, moving left to the right increases the sum.

options.text: Reset both pointers to the middle of the array.
options.explanation: Resetting pointers breaks the linear scan invariant.

options.text: Swap elements at the left and right pointer positions.
options.explanation: Swapping elements corrupts the sorted order of the collection.

questions.prompt: How does a sliding window update the sum of a fixed window of size k in O(1) time?

options.text: It multiplies the middle element by window length k.
options.explanation: Multiplying the middle element only works on arithmetic progressions.

options.text: It creates a concurrent task group to sum slice elements.
options.explanation: Creating concurrent tasks adds substantial thread overhead and is not O(1).

options.text: It adds the incoming element and subtracts the outgoing element.
options.explanation: Right. Adjusting only the boundary elements avoids recalculating the whole window.

options.text: It sorts the subarray and removes the smallest value.
options.explanation: Sorting the subarray takes O(k log k) time and destroys element order.

questions.prompt: What is the formula for the number of elements in a window from left to right inclusive?

options.text: right - left - 1
options.explanation: This expression undercounts window length by two.

options.text: right + left
options.explanation: Adding indices produces an arbitrary number unrelated to span length.

options.text: right - left
options.explanation: This formula undercounts the inclusive element count by one.

options.text: right - left + 1
options.explanation: Right. For inclusive bounds 0 through 2, 2 - 0 + 1 yields 3 elements.

questions.prompt: Why can repeatedly indexing a Swift String with offsetBy inside a loop cause O(n^2) time?

options.text: String indices are not random-access and each offset scan takes O(n) time.
options.explanation: Right. Grapheme clusters require linear traversal, making repeated indexing O(n^2).

options.text: Swift allocates a brand new String buffer on every subscript access.
options.explanation: Subscripting strings returns Character slices without cloning the whole buffer.

options.text: Strings in Swift are reference types requiring ARC atomic retain calls.
options.explanation: Swift String is a value type with copy-on-write semantics.

options.text: The compiler disables loop optimizations when using String.Index.
options.explanation: The slowdown stems from grapheme cluster traversal, not compiler flags.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended solution for two-pointer string problems in Swift interviews?

options.text: Force cast the String directly to an NSArray object.
options.explanation: Bridging to NSArray adds Objective-C overhead and loses Swift safety.

options.text: Convert the String to Array(string) once for O(1) integer access.
options.explanation: Right. Converting once takes O(n) time and grants O(1) random-access integer indexing.

options.text: Use NSString UTF-16 code unit offsets exclusively.
options.explanation: UTF-16 code units can split surrogate pairs and corrupt emoji characters.

options.text: Disable Unicode support by setting custom compiler flags.
options.explanation: Swift strings always preserve correct Unicode grapheme clusters.

questions.prompt: Why does a dynamic sliding window with an inner while loop have amortized O(n) time?

options.text: The Swift compiler unrolls all while loops into vector operations.
options.explanation: Loop unrolling is an optimization that does not change asymptotic complexity.

options.text: The while loop only executes when the right pointer reaches the end.
options.explanation: The while loop can execute during any iteration when constraints are violated.

options.text: Both left and right pointers only move forward and advance at most n times.
options.explanation: Right. Because pointers never move backward, total pointer steps cannot exceed 2n.

options.text: The while loop runs asynchronously on a background thread pool.
options.explanation: Sliding window algorithms run sequentially on a single thread.

questions.prompt: Which problem is best suited for the fast and slow pointer technique?

options.text: Calculating the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
options.explanation: Shortest path in unweighted graphs requires Breadth-First Search (BFS).

options.text: Balancing a binary search tree after node deletion.
options.explanation: Tree balancing uses tree rotations rather than pointer scanning.

options.text: Evaluating mathematical expressions in reverse Polish notation.
options.explanation: Expression evaluation uses a stack data structure.

options.text: Removing duplicate elements from a sorted array in-place.
options.explanation: Right. The slow pointer writes unique elements while the fast pointer scans ahead.

questions.prompt: What is the space complexity of removing duplicates in-place using two pointers?

options.text: O(1) auxiliary space because changes occur within the input array.
options.explanation: Right. Overwriting elements in-place requires only two index tracking variables.

options.text: O(n) space because Swift duplicates arrays on every mutation.
options.explanation: Passing arrays with inout avoids copying when only one reference exists.

options.text: O(k) space where k is the count of duplicate elements.
options.explanation: No extra buffer is created to store duplicate elements.

options.text: O(log n) space to maintain recursion stack frames.
options.explanation: Two pointers uses an iterative loop without recursion.

questions.prompt: Why should dynamic sliding windows shrink using a while loop rather than an if statement?

options.text: An if statement causes Swift to throw a compilation error.
options.explanation: Using an if statement is syntactically valid code but algorithmically flawed.

options.text: Adding one element may require contracting the window multiple times.
options.explanation: Right. A while loop ensures all invalid elements are removed until invariant holds.

options.text: A while loop forces the compiler to preallocate heap memory.
options.explanation: While loops manage control flow and do not allocate heap memory.

options.text: An if statement always resets the left pointer back to index 0.
options.explanation: An if statement advances by one step rather than resetting to 0.

questions.prompt: In Container With Most Water, why do we move the pointer pointing to the shorter line?

options.text: Because moving the taller line increases width automatically.
options.explanation: Moving either pointer decreases the width by 1 on every step.

options.text: Because the shorter line is swapped with the next element.
options.explanation: Container With Most Water inspects heights without modifying the array.

options.text: Because the shorter line limits area, and moving it is the only way to find a taller line.
options.explanation: Right. The shorter line caps capacity. Moving the taller line can only shrink area.

options.text: Because moving the shorter line resets the search interval.
options.explanation: Moving the shorter line narrows the interval inward rather than resetting.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between convergent two pointers and fast-and-slow pointers, including a problem for each. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Convergent two pointers start at opposite ends of an array and move inward. They are commonly used for palindrome checking or sorted Two Sum. In contrast, fast-and-slow pointers move in the same direction at different speeds. The fast pointer scans ahead while the slow pointer tracks boundaries or writes clean values, used for removing duplicates in-place.

rubric.criterion: Explains that convergent pointers start at opposite ends and move inward.
Explains that fast-and-slow pointers move in the same direction at different rates.
Provides an appropriate interview problem example for each technique.

questions.prompt: Explain how fixed-size sliding window achieves O(n) time and why it is faster than nested loops. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: A fixed-size sliding window calculates the initial sum of the first k elements in O(k) time. As it slides across the array, it updates the sum in O(1) time by adding the incoming element and subtracting the outgoing element. Nested loops recompute the entire window of size k at every position taking O(n * k) time. Sliding window avoids this redundant work to achieve linear O(n) time.

rubric.criterion: Explains that sliding window updates sums in O(1) by subtracting outgoing and adding incoming values.
Explains that nested loops recompute the entire window repeatedly in O(n * k) time.
States the resulting overall linear O(n) time complexity.

questions.prompt: Why can repeatedly indexing a Swift String inside a loop turn an O(n) algorithm into O(n^2), and how do you prevent this? Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Swift strings are composed of extended grapheme clusters rather than fixed-width characters. Because characters vary in byte length, computing string.index with an integer offset requires scanning from the beginning in O(n) time. Calling this inside a loop causes quadratic O(n^2) runtime. To prevent this, convert the String to an Array of characters once in O(n) time, enabling instant O(1) integer subscripting.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift string indices take O(n) time due to variable-width grapheme clusters.
Explains that repeated indexing inside a loop results in accidental O(n^2) quadratic time.
Recommends converting the string to Array(string) once for O(1) random-access indexing.

questions.prompt: Explain why dynamic sliding windows with an inner while loop run in amortized O(n) time rather than O(n^2). Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Even though a dynamic sliding window uses a while loop nested inside an outer loop, it runs in amortized O(n) time. The right pointer advances forward exactly n times to expand the window. The left pointer also only moves forward and never resets backward during window contraction. Because each element enters and leaves the window at most once, total operations are capped at 2n.

rubric.criterion: Explains that both left and right pointers only move forward and never reset backward.
States that each element enters and exits the window at most once, capping total steps at 2n.
Concludes that the total amortized time complexity is linear O(n).

questions.prompt: Explain the two-pointer decision rule in Container With Most Water and why moving the taller line can never produce a larger area. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: In Container With Most Water, the volume is determined by the formula: width multiplied by the shorter line height. On every step, moving either pointer decreases the width by one. If you move the taller line, the width decreases while the height remains capped by the existing shorter line, making a larger area impossible. Therefore, you must advance the pointer at the shorter line to seek a taller boundary.

rubric.criterion: Explains that area is constrained by the shorter line: width * min(height[left], height[right]).
Explains that moving the taller line reduces width without the possibility of increasing height limit.
Concludes that only moving the shorter pointer can potentially discover a larger area.
